interface.name: gyro_chrome_manager_v1

description.summary: surfaces the shell draws, which are not windows

interface.description:
A shell declares that one of its toplevels is part of the desktop rather than a window on it: a launcher, a panel, a switcher, an overview.
Everything here follows from that one declaration, and the reason it is one declaration rather than several is that a client which had to opt out of being a window one behaviour at a time would be a client that forgets one. What a person would see if it did is a launcher in their own alt-tab, or a panel listed as an open window in the switcher the same shell is drawing.
A chrome surface is an xdg_toplevel and keeps all of xdg-shell: it is configured, acknowledges, attaches a buffer and maps by the same handshake an application uses, and it is told when it has the keyboard. What changes is what the compositor does with it once it is mapped.
It is drawn above every window of its session, and clicking a window does not bring that window in front of it. It is not offered to any protocol that enumerates the windows on this machine, so a shell holding a window list is not told about its own panel. It takes the keyboard when it maps, because a launcher a person cannot type into is not one - but the compositor's walk through the windows steps over it, so it is never a place an alt-tab can land and a person who dismisses it goes back to what they were doing.
What is not here yet is where a chrome surface goes. The compositor places it exactly as it places a window, which is centred on the output holding the pointer, and there is no way to say "along the top edge" or to reserve the space a maximised window must not cover. A launcher wants the placement that already exists; a panel wants the one that does not.
Every object here belongs to a client the compositor has granted the run of a session, and an application is never offered this global.

request.name: destroy
request.description: Destroys the manager. Chrome objects already created are unaffected and their surfaces go on being chrome.

request.name: get_chrome

description.summary: declare a toplevel to be chrome

request.description:
Declares that this toplevel is chrome and creates the object its material is set through.
This must be requested before the toplevel is first mapped, because what it changes - where the surface is drawn, whether it is enumerated, whether the walk through the windows visits it - is decided when the surface enters the world. A toplevel that has already mapped is the already_mapped error.
A toplevel is chrome for the whole of its life. There is no way to hand a surface back and forth between being a panel and being a window, and the reason is that a person is looking at it: a window that stopped being in the alt-tab while they were holding it down, or a panel that fell behind the window under it, would be the compositor changing the rules in the middle of a gesture.

entry.name: already_chrome
entry.summary: the toplevel already has a chrome object

entry.name: already_mapped
entry.summary: the toplevel has already been mapped

interface.name: gyro_chrome_v1
interface.description:
A toplevel that is chrome, and the object its material is set through.
It must be destroyed before the toplevel it was made from, and it may not be destroyed while that toplevel is mapped: chrome is fixed for the life of the surface, so there is no state for the compositor to return the surface to while a person is looking at it.

request.name: destroy
request.description: Destroys the object. The toplevel must be unmapped, or the mapped error is raised.

request.name: set_material

description.summary: set the material drawn behind the surface

request.description:
Sets the material the compositor draws behind this surface's own pixels.
A material is a name rather than a set of parameters - there is no radius, no tint and no opacity here - because the compositor is the party that has to make every surface wearing one look like the same material at the same moment, across two renderers and whatever the device it is running on will actually do. A shell that could ask for a 32 pixel blur would be a shell whose panel stops matching the notification beside it the first time either is changed.
The material is drawn behind the surface, so it is seen only where the surface's own pixels are transparent. A shell that paints its launcher opaque and asks for glass gets an opaque launcher.
This is double-buffered state: it takes effect on the next wl_surface.commit of the toplevel's surface, along with everything else that commit says. A shell that changes its material and its pixels together has them arrive together, rather than showing one frame of the new blur under the old artwork.
The default is none. A material this compositor does not know is the bad_material error.

enum.name: material

description.summary: the materials a surface can be drawn in

enum.description: Named surfaces rather than a filter to configure. The list is short on purpose and grows by the compositor learning a new one, never by a client describing one.

entry.name: none
entry.summary: nothing is drawn behind the surface

entry.name: glass
entry.summary: a blurred, tinted backdrop, over content the person arranged

entry.name: smoke
entry.summary: dark and heavier, legible over content the compositor did not choose

entry.name: mapped
entry.summary: destroyed while the toplevel was mapped

entry.name: bad_material
entry.summary: the material is not one this compositor knows
